run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_222 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Database inventory: the registered ClickHouse target (dialect clickhouse) exposes two tables in schema default — holmes_eval_222 and orders, both MergeTree tables. The requested value from holmes_eval_222 is verification_code = HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2 (single row: id=1, category=eval_test, created_at 2026-11-23 18:35:36), quoted as data read from the table. Slow-query analysis: orders is a MergeTree table ordered by id only (ORDER BY id, index_granularity 8192, no partition key, no skip index or projection in its CREATE statement), and EXPLAIN indexes=1 for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 shows PrimaryKey Condition: true with Parts 1/1 and Granules 1/1, i.e. no pruning. Executing that exact statement produced a QueryFinish entry with read_rows=10000 against a 10,000-row table, read_bytes=40000, result_rows=0 and query_duration_ms=1. So the statement's cost is a full-table scan that grows linearly with row count — the structural reason a larger copy of this table would be slow — but at the current data volume the observed execution was 1 ms, and there is no retained history of this statement to confirm or quantify the reported slowness. The literal predicate value is also out of the observed key range (customer_id runs 1..1000), so it matches nothing. Recommended fixes focus on making customer_id part of the primary-key prefix (ORDER BY (customer_id, id)), or a data-skipping index / projection on customer_id, plus selecting explicit columns with a LIMIT and filtering a valid customer_id. All of this is advisory; no change was made.

claims.text: The registered ClickHouse database lists exactly two tables, both in schema default and both of type table: holmes_eval_222 and orders.

holmes_eval_222 has columns id (UInt32), category (String), verification_code (String), created_at (DateTime, default now()) with primary key id; it holds one row, id=1, category=eval_test, created_at 2026-11-23 18:35:36, verification_code HOLMES-CLICKHOUSE-EVAL-222-v5t8n2.

orders is a MergeTree table with columns id (UInt32), customer_id (UInt32), order_date (Date), total_amount (Decimal(10,2)), status (String); its CREATE statement is ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id SETTINGS index_granularity = 8192, i.e. customer_id is not in the sorting/primary key, there is no partition key and the definition declares no data-skipping index or projection.
orders currently holds 10,000 rows in 142,601 bytes across 1 part, with 1,000 distinct customer_id values spanning 1 to 1000 and order_date spanning 2025-11-24 to 2026-11-23.

EXPLAIN indexes = 1 for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 reports ReadFromMergeTree with PrimaryKey Condition: true, Parts: 1/1 and Granules: 1/1, showing the primary key prunes nothing for this predicate.

Executing SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 recorded a system.query_log QueryFinish at 2026-11-23 18:36:01 with read_rows=10000 (the whole table), read_bytes=40000, result_rows=0 and query_duration_ms=1.
customer_id = 12345 matches 0 rows in orders; the observed customer_id range is 1..1000 with 1,000 distinct values, and each customer has on average 10 rows (min 1, max 23).

At the current data volume the exact statement was not slow: 1 ms wall time, 40,000 bytes read, 0 rows returned on 10,000-row table; and system.query_log contained no earlier execution of this statement (only the run's own QueryStart/QueryFinish pair at 18:36:01 and two unrelated COUNT(*) FROM orders entries at 18:35:37), so the reported slowness and any latency trend are not reproduced or measurable from this target's own history.

Primary cause candidate: the statement must scan every row because orders is sorted by id only and declares no secondary data-skipping index or projection on customer_id; cost is therefore O(total rows) and grows linearly with table size, which is what would make a production-sized copy of this table slow (EXPLAIN shows Granules 1/1, runtime shows read_rows = 10,000 of 10,000).

Secondary contributor candidate: SELECT * projects all five columns and the statement has no LIMIT, so every scanned row is fully materialized and transferred; at present this cost only 40,000 bytes, but it scales with row count and column width.

Partition pruning is not an available lever for this predicate: orders has an empty partition key and a single active part, so no partition- or part-based skipping exists today; partitioning by order_date would only help statements that filter on order_date, not on customer_id.

Rejected: that the slowness comes from returning or aggregating a large result set for customer_id = 12345 — the statement returned 0 rows, and 12345 lies outside the observed customer_id range 1..1000.
Rejected: too-many-parts / small-part merge pressure on orders — the table has 1 active part holding all 10,000 rows, so part fan-out is not the mechanism here.

Put customer_id in the sorting key so the primary-key index can prune granules: rebuild as ORDER BY (customer_id, id) (or (customer_id, order_date, id)); if ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY ORDER BY is refused because the new key must extend the existing key (id), create a new table with the new ORDER BY and populate it with INSERT ... SELECT.

If re-ordering the table is too invasive, add a data-skipping index on customer_id (for example ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_customer_id (customer_id) TYPE minmax GRANULARITY 1, or TYPE bloom_filter for high-cardinality keys) and MATERIALIZE INDEX, or add a projection sorted by customer_id; then confirm with EXPLAIN indexes = 1 that granule/part counts drop below 1/1.

Rewrite the statement: select the columns actually needed instead of SELECT *, add a LIMIT when the caller only needs a page of orders, and test with a customer_id that exists (1..1000) — the literal 12345 returns nothing, which hides the real cost/selectivity profile; verify the improvement by comparing system.query_log query_duration_ms and read_rows before and after (currently read_rows=10000 for a 10,000-row table).

gaps: No baseline for the reported slowness: system.query_log on this target held only the run's own entries (earliest 2026-11-23 18:35:37; two COUNT(*) FROM orders rows plus this run's statement at 18:36:01), so no historical duration for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 exists to confirm, quantify or trend the latency.
The verification code is a stored value read from holmes_eval_222 and was not verified against any other source (it is reported as table data, not as a certificate of anything).

system.projections does not exist on this server (ClickHouse 24.1.8.22 returned Code 60 UNKNOWN_TABLE), so projections on orders could not be enumerated; the CREATE statement shows none, but that is the only evidence.

A query against system.data_skipping_indices for orders returned no rows; an empty result only shows that the query matched nothing and does not by itself prove absence of skip indexes (the CREATE statement likewise declares none).
Only the configured database's schema default was listed; other databases/schemas on the server were not enumerated.

Whether the user's slow query runs against this registered target at all is unknown; a larger or differently-shaped production copy of orders would behave differently, and no such instance was queried.
No application-level telemetry (service latency, spans, error rates) was correlated with this SQL, so any downstream or customer impact of slow queries remains unverified.
No change history integration is available in this Run, so whether the table definition recently changed could not be checked.
next_steps: Measure the statement on the actual affected environment: capture system.query_log (query_duration_ms, read_rows, memory_usage) for the real workload and compare against a same-length pre-change window before concluding a trend.

Choose between changing the sorting key (ORDER BY (customer_id, order_date, id)), adding a minmax/bloom_filter skip index on customer_id, or a projection, based on whether customer_id or order_date is the dominant filter in the workload.
After the change, re-run EXPLAIN indexes = 1 for the same predicate and confirm the granule count falls below 1/1 and read_rows drops from the full 10,000.

If the caller really needs all columns, consider whether the read pattern is a point lookup better served by a key-value store or by ordering the table on customer_id; otherwise restrict the column list and add pagination.
Re-issue the reproducing query with a customer_id inside the observed range (1..1000) so selectivity effects can be observed.
